place.zh: 沂中医 · 体育馆新地板 · 十二月
place.en: Yizhong · the new gym floor · December

setup.zh: 解剖台上脊梁两边那一串小结，「它只认一句话：要出事了」；露天场子十投七，新地板上全队围着喊十投二；手环一百一十二，「它分不清看台和野地」，吐气刹得住一截、刹不干净。《养性延命录》长息那一句旁的铅笔字：「临考前夜试之，手犹颤。然下笔矣。」手札：「怕的时候，先吐一口长气。」阿禾：「手的事，交给手。」
setup.en: The chain of little knots beside the spine on the anatomy table: "it answers to one sentence: something's about to happen." Seven of ten on the open court; two of ten on the new floor with the team yelling. 112 on the band: "It can't tell the stands from the wild"; a breath out brakes part of it, not all. The pencil beside the "long breath" line: "Tried it the night before the exam; hand still shook. But the pen came down." The journal: "When afraid, first let out one long breath." Ahe: "The hands' business, leave to the hands."

recap.zh: 一个人十投七，十一个人围着喊十投二；怕是一脚油门，吐气刹得住一截。
recap.en: Seven of ten alone, two of ten with eleven yelling; fear is a foot on the gas, and a breath out brakes only part of it.

en: Seven of ten. Two of ten.

story.zh:
零点六秒，落后一分，两个罚球——全场几百双眼睛等着看的，是一个上场概率百分之一的人的手。

那双手五天前还是准的。

十二月三日起，他在体育场边上那片露天场子上顶着北风投罚球，一天两百个。头三天是阿禾在场边数；第四天起，六一七全体出动：眼镜站在篮下捡球，老蔡站在线边递球，递一个，念一个一食堂的菜名，说是给他「补一补」——念到第五十个，一食堂的菜用完了，改念二食堂的。露天场子的灯十点关，关了灯三个人摸黑往回走，老蔡还在念：「锅包肉。」

没几天，食堂后门的红薯也来了。它脑门上那撮毛立着，蹲在铁丝网外头看了半天，不知怎么钻了进来，往篮下一蹲。球砸筐弹出来，它「嗖」地蹿出去，叼——球太大，叼不住，便拿脑袋顶，一路顶回罚球线，顶到沈芒脚边，坐下，尾巴摇成了一朵花，等着夸。眼镜道：「它捡得比我快。」从那天起，篮下归了红薯，眼镜改去场边背单词。只有一样不好：投进的球，它也要追，追到了还不给。

阿禾来看过一回，裹着羽绒服站在铁丝网外头，本子摊在网上。他投十个，她不看球进不进，看他的嘴。「吐了。」「吐了。」「这个没吐。」十个投完，她把本子合上：「进不进是手的事。吐不吐是你的事。」说完走了。眼镜在篮下道：「她数的不是球。」沈芒道：「我知道。」

下午两点，实验楼五楼，解剖实验室。

那位说话很轻的女老师拿镊子指着肾上头一小片黄黄的、软软的东西，像肾戴了一顶歪着的小帽子：「肾上腺。帽子里头有一芯子，专管往血里放一样东西。」镊子往里挪，挪到脊梁骨两边，「它听谁的？听这一串的。」

脊梁骨两边，各有一条细细的线，一节一个小疙瘩，从上头一直排到骨盆里去，又细又匀，像一串穿好的珠子。

「这一串，从脖子排到骨盆，每一节一个小结。人一吓，脑子一声令下，这一串一齐动：心跳快，瞳孔开，手心出汗，唾沫停，血从肚子里往胳膊腿上调；帽子里那一芯子再往血里挤一把，把这一套顶到头。」她顿了顿，「它只认一句话：要出事了。什么事，它不问。」

她叫人上来，戴着手套，拿指头顺着那一串轻轻摸一摸。轮到沈芒，他按下去——不像肉，倒像一根细绳子上打了一溜小结，硬硬的，一节一节。他按着那一溜小结，想起了十月里对抗赛那两个罚球：嘴干，手抖，心跳快得像楼上有人跺地板——原来在这儿。阿禾教他的吸四拍吐六拍，她管那叫踩刹车；原来刹车踩的，是在跟这一串抢。

「老师，」沈芒举手，「它分得清……比方说，考试跟老虎吗？」

后排有人笑了一声。老师没笑，看了他一眼——她认得这个人，这一学期问得最多的就是他。「分不清。」她道，「它比你的脑子快。脑子还没想明白是什么事，它已经动手了。」她把镊子放下，「叫它慢下来的那一路，另有一根，不在今天的台子上。下学期生理学细讲。」

傍晚五点，冬训摸底。球馆还在换地板，测的是露天场子。北风把篮网刮得横着飘，阿禾裹着羽绒服，本子摊在膝盖上，一样一样来：称，量，跑，投。

一千米他跑了四分零八。九月十一号那天，是四分五十八。阿禾把秒表按停，没说好，也没说不好，只报了一句：「四分零八。」他弯着腰喘，喘得很深，一口顶一口；听见这个数，他直起腰来，北风里脸上发烫。三个月，五十秒。

最后是罚球。十个。老蔡在线边递球，眼镜在篮下，红薯坐在眼镜脚边——投进的它不追了，只追砸筐的。十投七。

阿禾的本子上只有一行：「沈芒　罚球 十投七。」

她合上本子：「替补席上，你最准。」

他先是高兴，高兴完了，心里「咯噔」一下：替补席上最准，那就是说，要是真到了那一步……他没敢往下想。

十六日，球馆的新地板铺好了，院队头一回回到馆里练。漆味儿冲鼻子，灯一打，地板亮得照得见人影。练到最后半个钟头，阿禾把本子一合：「练罚球。一个人站线上，其余的人，围着喊。」

从十一月起，全队天天站在底线上看他罚十个，看是看惯了；喊，是头一回。大刘头一个上，十一个人围着他又拍手又跺脚，有人拿两只鞋底子对着拍，拍得震天响；大刘十投六，投完了冲围着的人嚷：「你们喊得不够响！响点我能进八个！」队长邢斌上，十投八，一句话没有。轮到沈芒，他往线上一站，还没拿到球，耳朵先红了。

十一个人一齐喊起来。老蔡不是队里的人，蹲在门口看热闹，也跟着喊了一嗓子：「零号，你倒是投啊！」

他投了十个，一个比一个快，昨天夜里还记得的那口气，这回连吐都忘了吐。进了两个。

露天场子上，北风里，一个人，十投七；新地板上，十一个人围着喊，十投二。手是同一双手，球是同一个球，篮筐一寸也没变。

散了以后，他一个人坐在场边解鞋带。阿禾走过来，在本子上写完了那一行，没给他看，只道：「差的那五个，不在手上。」

「那在哪儿？」

阿禾想了想，没有答。她把本子夹在胳膊底下，走到门口，又回过头来：「十九号，要是到了那一步，你也是这么喊着的。」

那天夜里，六一七做了一个实验。主意是眼镜出的：「你坐着别动，我们喊，看你的手环。」沈芒盘腿坐在下铺，一动不动，手环上的数平平稳稳。老蔡清了清嗓子，凑到他耳朵边上，用尽平生之力，唾沫星子喷了他半边脸：「零号！百分之一！」

沈芒眼皮都没眨。手环上的数，一跳一跳，跳到了一百一十二。

三个人对着那个数看了半天。眼镜道：「你一步没跑，心跳得跟爬了五层楼一样。一嗓子，就是一脚油门踩到底。」老蔡道：「我嗓子好。」

沈芒没理他们。他盯着那个一百一十二，想起下午台子上那一串小结：要出事了，什么事，它不问。看台和野地，它分不清。原来不是手不行，是身子以为要出事了。

「那怎么关？」

眼镜扶了扶眼镜：「关不了。下午老师说了，它比你脑子快。」

「再来一回。」沈芒道，「这回我吐气。」

老蔡又凑上来，又是一嗓子。沈芒闭上眼，吸四拍，吐六拍，吐得慢，慢得老蔡第二嗓子都喊完了，他那口气还没吐完。三个人盯着手环。那个数掉了一截，掉到一半上下，不掉了，就在那儿一跳一跳。

「刹得住一截，」眼镜道，「刹不干净。」

「那剩下那一截呢？」

眼镜想了想，没答。那天夜里沈芒躺在下铺，手环早摘了，可他觉得那剩下的一截还在胸口里一跳一跳，跟他一块儿躺着。

十七日，礼拜四，上午第一节还是针灸推拿学导论。严老师下课前没默写，只在黑板上写了一行：「12月22日（冬至）调课，期末前最后一次默写：十二正经，写名字，写走向。」粉笔头在「走向」上敲了两下：「一条不许少。」眼镜在旁边小声道：「还有五天。」名字他九月里就背下了；连走向一块儿背得下的，沈芒在桌肚里数了数：九条。另外三条，跟礼拜六一样，都在等他。

下午他又去了古籍部。葛奶奶正拿铅笔在一张借阅卡上描字，一进门便从老花镜上头看他：「要比赛了？脸跟纸一样。」

他在桌边坐下，闭上眼，想什么也不想。头一秒，他想到了「什么也不想」这几个字；第二秒，想到了表白墙上那个「1%」；第三秒，想到了马小宝那只咯吱咯吱的大摇杯；第五秒，他已经站在罚球线上了，看台上几百双眼睛，一齐盯着他的手。他「腾」地睁开眼，一身冷汗。

葛奶奶头也不抬：「越不想，越想。我年轻时候也这样。」

他请葛奶奶捧出九月里那一函《养性延命录》，翻到讲吐气的那一页。上回他只顾着看页边，这回看了正文：

「凡行气，以鼻内气，以口吐气，微而引之，名曰长息。」

他罚球出手前吐的那一口，原来有名字。这一句的页边，「试之。吐长于纳，心果缓。」那一行底下，还有一行铅笔批注，跟上头是一个人的手笔，字小而急，淡得快看不见了：

「临考前夜试之，手犹颤。然下笔矣。」

沈芒对着这行字看了很久。手还是抖的，可是笔落下去了。他不知道写这行字的人考的是什么，考过了没有。他只知道，几十年前，有个人跟他一样怕过，怕着怕着，把笔落下去了。

取包的时候，他又蹲到门边那架矮书架前头，从那一函厚书里抽出手札的头一册，翻到靠后的一页：「十九岁九月初三，崖顶。见一门，门上有字。怕。」底下另起一行：「怕的时候，先吐一口长气。」

这老头也怕过。他把这两行抄进了手机备忘录，抄完了，又把「先吐一口长气」单独抄了一遍。

十八日中午，一食堂，他碰见了马小宝。马小宝面前摆着三个餐盘，吃得只剩下盘子，正抹着嘴往窗口走，看样子要去打第四盘。路过沈芒的桌子，他停了一停，从沈芒盘子里拈起一个鸡蛋，在手心里掂了掂。鸡蛋在他手心里轻轻地磕，磕了两下——那只手在抖。十二月的食堂，他额头上一层汗。沈芒看着那只手，想起停电那一夜黑地里的腕子，嘴张了张，没出声。马小宝把鸡蛋放回去：「零号，明天我站篮下。你站哪儿？」不等他答，自己先笑了，「哦，对，板凳。板凳好，板凳不晃。」

沈芒低头剥鸡蛋。马小宝走出去两步，又回过头来：「对了，明晚有直播，学校公众号上挂着呢。全校都看。小意思。」

沈芒剥着剥着，蛋白上剥出了一个坑。

那天下午是决赛前最后一练。散了以后，阿禾走到罚球线上，他正站在那儿，球抱在怀里，没投。

「北风里两千多个，」她道，「手记住了没有？」

「记住了。」

「那到了那一步，别想手。」她拿笔点了点他的胸口，「你想的，只有一样：吐。拍两下，吐，屈膝，抬手——手的事，交给手。熟了的东西，抖着也做得出来；不熟的，不抖也做不出来。」

「要是手不听呢？」

「那就记：手不听。」她把笔帽按上，「你练的不是不抖。你练的是，抖着也投。」

十点，他妈在家长群里发了一条消息，配着一个链接：「明晚七点，学校篮球决赛直播。0号是我儿子。」不到十分钟，底下回了三十七个「加油」，一个「孩子长高了」，还有一个问：「是不是跑一千米那个？」他妈回：「是。」

沈芒「呜——」地一声，把脑袋蒙进被子里，两条腿在被窝里乱蹬。现在好了：看台上的几百个人，表白墙上的几千个人，再加上家长群里一百多位叔叔阿姨，还有他爸。蹬够了，他躺在被子里不动了，这才明白，他怕的不光是投不进——是投不进的时候，这么多人正好都在看。

快十二点，他给阿禾发：「要是真到那一步，我投不进，怎么办？」

那头「正在输入」了很久，停了，又输入，又停了。最后来了一句：「那我就记：投不进。」隔了一会儿，又一句：「记下来的，丢不了。」
story.en:
Zero point six seconds, down by one, two free throws — what hundreds of pairs of eyes in the gym were waiting to see was the hands of someone with a one percent chance of playing.

Five days earlier, those hands had been accurate.

From December 3rd he'd been shooting free throws on the open court beside the stadium, into the north wind, two hundred a day. For the first three days Ahe counted from the sideline; from the fourth, all of Room 617 turned out: Specs under the basket rebounding, Old Cai at the line feeding him the ball — and with every ball, the name of a dish from the First Canteen, to "build him up"; by the fiftieth the First Canteen's menu ran out, and he moved on to the Second. The outdoor lights went off at ten; the three of them walked back in the dark, Old Cai still reciting: "Sweet and sour pork."

Within a few days Sweet Potato from the canteen's back door came too. That tuft of fur standing up on his forehead, he squatted outside the wire fence watching for a long while, somehow squeezed through, and sat down under the basket. When a ball hit the rim and bounced out he shot after it — too big to carry in his mouth, so he nosed it all the way back to the free-throw line, up to Shen Mang's feet, sat down, tail wagging like a pinwheel, and waited to be praised. Specs said, "He fetches faster than I do." From that day the basket belonged to Sweet Potato, and Specs moved to the sideline to memorize vocabulary. The one drawback: he chased the ones that went in too, and once he caught them he wouldn't give them back.

Ahe came to watch once, bundled in her down jacket outside the wire fence, her notebook open against the mesh. He shot ten; she didn't watch whether they went in, she watched his mouth. "Breathed out." "Breathed out." "That one, no." When the ten were done she closed the notebook: "Whether it goes in is the hands' business. Whether you breathe out is yours." And she left. Specs said from under the basket, "She's not counting the ball." Shen Mang said, "I know."

Two in the afternoon, fifth floor of the lab building, the anatomy lab.

The teacher with the quiet voice pointed her forceps at a small, yellowish, soft thing on top of the kidney, as if the kidney were wearing a little cap set askew: "The adrenal gland. There's a core inside the cap whose one job is to release a certain thing into the blood." The forceps moved inward, to either side of the spine. "And who does it take orders from? From this chain."

On either side of the spine ran a fine line, a little knot at each segment, running from the top all the way down into the pelvis, fine and even, like a string of threaded beads.

"This chain runs from the neck to the pelvis, one little knot per segment. When a person is frightened, the brain gives one order and the whole chain moves at once: the heart speeds up, the pupils open, the palms sweat, the saliva stops, blood is pulled from the belly out to the arms and legs; then that core inside the cap squeezes one more dose into the blood and pushes the whole thing to the top." She paused. "It answers to one sentence only: something's about to happen. What — it doesn't ask."

She called them up, gloved, to run a finger lightly along the chain. When it was Shen Mang's turn he pressed down — not like flesh; more like a thin cord with a row of knots tied in it, hard, one after another. Pressing on that row of knots, he thought of the two free throws in the October scrimmage: dry mouth, shaking hands, his heart going like someone stamping on the floor upstairs — so this was where it lived. The four-in, six-out Ahe had taught him, she called it stepping on the brake; so what the brake was pressing against was this chain.

"Teacher," Shen Mang raised his hand, "can it tell the difference... say, between an exam and a tiger?"

Someone at the back laughed. The teacher didn't. She looked at him — she knew this one; he'd asked more questions this semester than anyone. "It can't." she said. "It's faster than your brain. Before the brain has worked out what's happening, it has already acted." She set the forceps down. "The route that slows it down again is a different nerve, and it isn't on today's table. Physiology next semester."

Five in the evening, the winter-training baseline test. The gym floor was still being replaced, so it was held on the open court. The north wind had the nets flying sideways; Ahe was bundled in her down jacket, notebook open on her knees, taking them one by one: weigh, measure, run, shoot.

He ran the thousand meters in four minutes eight. On September 11th it had been four fifty-eight. Ahe stopped the watch, said neither good nor bad, only reported: "Four-oh-eight." He was bent over, breathing hard but deep, one breath on top of the last; when he heard the number he straightened up, and in the north wind his face burned. Three months, fifty seconds.

Last came the free throws. Ten. Old Cai feeding him at the line, Specs under the basket, Sweet Potato sitting at Specs's feet — he no longer chased the ones that went in, only the ones that hit the rim. Seven of ten.

Ahe's notebook had just one line: "Shen Mang  free throws 7 of 10."

She closed the notebook: "Of everyone on the bench, you're the most accurate."

At first he was pleased; then his heart gave a lurch: the most accurate on the bench meant that if it really came to that... He didn't dare think any further.

On the 16th, the gym's new floor was finished and the college team came back indoors for the first time. The varnish stung the nose; with the lights on, the floor was bright enough to show your reflection. For the last half hour Ahe snapped her notebook shut: "Free-throw practice. One person on the line, everyone else around him, yelling."

Since November the whole team had stood on the baseline every day watching him shoot ten; watching they were used to. Yelling was new. Big Liu went first, eleven people around him clapping and stamping, someone slapping two shoe soles together loud enough to shake the roof; Big Liu, six of ten, and when he was done he yelled at the circle, "You're not loud enough! Louder and I'd make eight!" The captain, Xing Bin, went next: eight of ten, without a word. Then Shen Mang. The moment he stepped to the line, before he even had the ball, his ears went red.

Eleven people yelled at once. Old Cai wasn't on the team; he was squatting in the doorway watching the fun, and he threw in a shout too: "Number Zero, just shoot it!"

He shot ten, each one faster than the last; the breath he'd still remembered the night before, this time he forgot even to let out. Two went in.

On the outdoor court, in the north wind, alone: seven of ten. On the new floor, with eleven people yelling around him: two of ten. The same pair of hands, the same ball; the rim hadn't moved an inch.

When it broke up he sat alone at the side untying his laces. Ahe came over, finished writing her line, didn't show it to him, and said only: "The five you're missing aren't in your hands."

"Then where?"

Ahe thought about it and didn't answer. She tucked the notebook under her arm, walked to the door, and turned back: "On the nineteenth, if it comes to that, this is how they'll be yelling at you."

That night Room 617 ran an experiment. The idea was Specs's: "You sit still, we yell, and we watch your band." Shen Mang sat cross-legged on the lower bunk without moving, the number on his fitness band flat and steady. Old Cai cleared his throat, leaned in to his ear and shouted with all the strength he had, spraying spit over half his face: "Number Zero! One percent!"

Shen Mang didn't even blink. The number on the band jumped and jumped, up to one hundred and twelve.

The three of them stared at the number for a long time. Specs said, "You haven't run a single step, and your heart's going like you just climbed five flights of stairs. One yell, and it floors the gas." Old Cai said, "I've got a good voice."

Shen Mang ignored them. He stared at the one hundred and twelve and thought of the chain of little knots on the table that afternoon: something's about to happen — what, it doesn't ask. The stands or the wild, it can't tell. So it wasn't that his hands were no good: his body thought something was about to happen.

"So how do you switch it off?"

Specs pushed up his glasses: "You can't. The teacher said it this afternoon: it's faster than your brain."

"Once more," Shen Mang said. "This time I breathe out."

Old Cai leaned in again, another shout. Shen Mang closed his eyes: in for four, out for six, so slowly that Old Cai had finished a second shout before the breath was done. Three of them stared at the band. The number dropped a step, down to about half, and stopped there, ticking.

"It brakes part of it," Specs said. "Not all of it."

"And the part that's left?"

Specs thought, and had no answer. That night Shen Mang lay on the lower bunk with the band long since off, and still felt that leftover part ticking in his chest, lying there with him.

The 17th, Thursday, first period was still Introduction to Acupuncture and Tuina. Teacher Yan gave no dictation before the bell; he only wrote one line on the board: "Dec 22 (winter solstice), class rescheduled; last dictation before finals: the twelve regular meridians, names and courses." He tapped the chalk twice on "courses": "Not one less." Specs said quietly beside him, "Five days." The names he had learned back in September; the ones he could recite with their courses, Shen Mang counted under the desk: nine. The other three, like Saturday, were waiting for him.

In the afternoon he went to the Rare Books Room again. Granny Ge was tracing letters on a loan card with a pencil, and looked at him over her reading glasses the moment he came in: "Got a game coming up? Your face is as white as paper."

He sat down at a table, closed his eyes, and tried to think of nothing. In the first second he thought of the words "think of nothing"; in the second, of the "1%" on the confessions wall; in the third, of Ma Xiaobao's big creaking shaker; by the fifth he was already standing on the free-throw line, hundreds of eyes in the stands fixed on his hands. His eyes flew open, and he was in a cold sweat.

Granny Ge didn't look up: "The harder you try not to think, the more you think. I was like that when I was young."

He asked Granny Ge to bring out the September case of *Records of Nourishing Nature and Prolonging Life* and turned to the page on breathing out. Last time he had only looked at the margin; this time he read the text:

"In all circulation of qi, take the breath in through the nose and let it out through the mouth, faintly, drawing it long; this is called the long breath."

So the breath he let out before every free throw had a name. In the margin beside that sentence, under the line "Tried it. Out longer than in; the heart did slow," was one more line of pencil, in the same hand, small and hurried, so faint it was almost gone:

"Tried it the night before the exam. My hand still shook. But the pen came down."

Shen Mang looked at that line for a long time. The hand still shook, but the pen came down. He didn't know what exam the writer had sat, or whether he'd passed. He only knew that decades ago, someone had been as scared as he was — and scared as he was, had brought the pen down.

Collecting his bag, he crouched again at the low bookcase by the door, drew the first volume of the journal out of its case of thick books and turned to a page near the back: "Age nineteen, third day of the ninth month. The clifftop. Saw a door, with writing on it. Afraid." Below, on a new line: "When afraid, first let out one long breath."

So this old man had been afraid too. He copied both lines into his phone notes, and when he had, copied "first let out one long breath" once more on its own.

At noon on the 18th, in the First Canteen, he ran into Ma Xiaobao. Three trays sat in front of him, eaten down to the plates; he was wiping his mouth and heading for the counter, apparently for a fourth. Passing Shen Mang's table he paused, picked an egg off his plate, weighed it in his palm. The egg tapped against his palm, twice — the hand was shaking. In a December canteen, his forehead was beaded with sweat. Shen Mang looked at that hand, thought of the wrist in the dark on the night of the blackout, opened his mouth, and said nothing. Ma Xiaobao put the egg back: "Number Zero, tomorrow I'm under the basket. Where are you?" He answered himself before Shen Mang could, laughing: "Oh, right — the bench. The bench is good. The bench doesn't wobble."

Shen Mang kept his head down, peeling the egg. Ma Xiaobao took two steps and turned back: "Oh, and tomorrow night's livestreamed, it's up on the school's official account. The whole school's watching. No big deal."

He peeled and peeled, and peeled a hole in the white.

That afternoon was the last practice before the final. When it broke up, Ahe walked to the free-throw line, where he was standing with the ball hugged to his chest, not shooting.

"Two thousand-odd in the north wind," she said. "Have the hands remembered?"

"They have."

"Then if it comes to that, don't think about the hands." She tapped his chest with her pen. "You think about one thing only: the breath out. Two bounces, breathe out, bend the knees, raise the hands — the hands' business, leave to the hands. What's practiced, you can do even shaking; what isn't, you can't do even steady."

"And if the hands won't listen?"

"Then I write it down: hands didn't listen." She clicked the cap back on. "What you're training isn't not shaking. What you're training is shooting while you shake."

At ten, his mom posted in the parents' group, with a link: "Tomorrow at seven, the school basketball final is livestreamed. Number 0 is my son." Within ten minutes there were thirty-seven "Go for it!"s, one "He's grown taller," and one asking: "Is that the one from the thousand meters?" His mom replied: "Yes."

Shen Mang let out a "Waaah—", pulled the covers over his head, and kicked his legs wildly under the quilt. Now he had it all: the hundreds in the stands, the thousands on the confessions wall, a hundred-odd aunties and uncles in the parents' group, and his dad. When he was done kicking he lay still under the quilt, and only then understood: what scared him wasn't just missing — it was that when he missed, all these people would be watching.

Near midnight, he messaged Ahe: "If it really comes to that and I miss, what do I do?"

On her end, "typing…" went on for a long time, stopped, started, stopped again. At last one line came: "Then I'll write down: missed." A while later, another: "What gets written down doesn't get lost."
